scenes.title: Find Settings from the Records Manage menu

captions.text: Records administration starts with finding the correct controls.
In the Records area, open All records and choose Manage.
The expanded menu contains Settings and Definitions.
Settings holds department-level values; Definitions lets you inspect
the forms and their own policies.
Begin with Settings.
This example uses the fictional Firehouse fifty-one training department,
so the practice changes stay with a separate training environment.

captions.text: Scroll to the bottom of Records Settings.
Save and Cancel are visible below the other settings sections.
Review the intended change, then choose Save once.
Typing a value into a field only prepares the form.
The returned page and a fresh page load give you a separate
check that the intended values were accepted and retained.
The returned page displays Records settings saved.
The lifecycle field shows Review Required, and the review deadline shows forty-eight.
Compare both saved values with the two values you intended to change.
A success notice helps, and inspecting the fields confirms which
configuration is now displayed.
Reopening Records Settings shows Review Required and forty-eight hours again.
This is a fresh page load after the save.
It confirms that the department form retained those values.
The next check is the policy on existing record definitions.
A saved department value alone does not tell you the lifecycle shown by
every form that personnel can use.

scenes.title: Return to Manage and open Definitions

captions.text: Return to All records and expand Manage again.
Choose Definitions from this menu to inspect the record forms.
This keeps the department settings check separate from the definition
check, while giving administrators a repeatable route to both screens.
The Definitions table includes Owner, Published version and
Lifecycle preset columns.
Run and Training are marked Product, locked.
Both show published version one and Quick Entry.
This screen was captured while the department form had the
saved Review Required value.
The locked definitions still show their own Quick Entry policy, matching the scope
described in the department settings help.
Read the row you actually intend to use.
In the same table, locate Training Only, Community software exercise.
Its owner is Department, and its lifecycle column shows Quick Entry.
The row has an Edit link.
Choose Edit to inspect that definition version.
Use the definition name and owner to distinguish a department-owned form from
a locked product form before deciding which policy you are maintaining.

scenes.title: Prepare the original values for restoration

captions.text: Return to Records Settings after the exercise.
The prepared restoration selects Quick Entry and enters seventy-two
hours, matching the baseline.
Compare both fields with the values you recorded at the start.
Restoring a practice change should be an intentional configuration
decision, using the same review of the complete form as the original change.

scenes.title: Use Save for the restoration too

captions.text: Use the same Save action at the bottom of the settings
form to apply the restoration.
The original values are still only prepared until you save them.
Verify the returned result before ending the exercise.
Records settings saved appears again.
Quick Entry and seventy-two hours are now displayed on the returned form.
The demonstration has restored its original department defaults.
No record was submitted for review, and no definition version was edited or
published during this settings exercise.

scenes.title: Apply the verification process to your department

captions.text: A final reopening still shows Quick Entry and seventy-two hours.
Use this same baseline, save, reopen and definition-inspection
process for your department.
Security teams can organize post-report review, wildland contractors can review
crew-support records, and industrial teams can coordinate exercise documentation.
Community paramedicine and mental health teams can define appropriate
outreach review responsibilities, while search-and-rescue teams can
review mission-support documentation.
Fire and E M S departments can use the same checks.
Set a clear policy, then verify the specific form personnel will use.
